question: What is the main goal of the Essential Drug Programme?

options.A: To restrict patient access to common over-the-counter drugs
options.B: To make safe and effective medicines affordable and available
options.C: To eliminate the need for international pharmaceutical trade
options.D: To promote expensive brand-name pharmaceuticals in hospitals

explanation: You got this! The core idea is simple: making sure everyday life-saving medicines remain cheap enough and within reach for everyone who needs them.

question: Why does the Essential Drug Programme focus heavily on generic medicines instead of brand names?

options.A: Generics are generally much more affordable and optimize limited health budgets
options.B: Brand-name drugs are scientifically proven to be unsafe for public use
options.C: International law forbids developing nations from buying brand names
options.D: Generic medicines work faster in acute emergency conditions

explanation: Spot on! Generic drugs save money, helping clinics stretch tight budgets to treat more patients without cutting corners on quality.

question: When did the World Health Organization (WHO) publish its first Model List of Essential Medicines?
explanation: Great try! The WHO put out this very first list back in 1977 to bring order, safety, and priority to global drug markets.

question: What was the main problem in drug markets before the WHO introduced essential drug guidelines?

options.A: Patients refused to take any form of modern medical treatment
options.B: There were absolute shortages of chemical factories globally
options.C: Governments completely banned the importation of foreign drugs
options.D: Markets were flooded with too many unverified and expensive drug formulations

explanation: Well done! Back then, the market was chaotic with countless pricey products of doubtful quality, which confused doctors and drained wallets.

question: Which factor is most important when deciding if a medicine belongs on an essential drug list?

options.A: How recently the drug was invented in a laboratory
options.B: National disease prevalence and public health needs
options.C: The marketing budget of the manufacturing company
options.D: Whether the drug is packaged in a colorful container

explanation: Exactly! We pick drugs based on the actual illnesses that trouble our local communities the most.

question: A hospital committee is choosing between a brand-new, super expensive painkiller and an older, cheap one that works almost as well. What should they do?

options.A: Stock it only for patients who complain about older drugs
options.B: Buy large quantities to impress visiting health inspectors
options.C: Accept it immediately to stay modern and technologically advanced
options.D: Reject it because it fails the cost-effectiveness principle

explanation: You nailed it! As nurses and health planners, we always balance the health benefit against the cost to ensure wise spending.

question: What is a major benefit of having a standard list of medications in a clinic?

options.A: It guarantees that pharmaceutical companies make higher profits
options.B: It forces patients to buy medications outside the hospital
options.C: It reduces dispensing errors and simplifies inventory management
options.D: It completely eliminates the need for qualified pharmacists

explanation: That's right! Using a smaller, familiar group of drugs keeps storage organized and helps prevent medication mix-ups.

question: Which of these is NOT a standard rule when picking essential medicines?

options.A: Proven clinical effectiveness in human trials
options.B: Affordability for the target patient population
options.D: The aesthetic appeal of the product packaging

explanation: Correct! A pretty wrapper doesn't make a drug safer or more effective for our patients.

question: Which Nigerian agency works closely with the Ministry of Health to regulate and oversee drug standards?
explanation: You know this! NAFDAC is our frontline agency in Nigeria keeping fake and unsafe drugs away from our people.

question: Why does the National Essential Medicines List divide drugs by levels of healthcare (like PHCs vs teaching hospitals)?

options.A: To restrict advanced medical care exclusively to politicians and the wealthy
options.B: To match drug availability with the clinical competence and needs of each facility type
options.C: To ensure that primary health centers have the most expensive drugs first
options.D: To make record-keeping as difficult as possible for rural nurses

explanation: Spot on! Basic health centers stock what nurses can safely give, while complex specialist drugs go to advanced teaching hospitals.

question: What is a major danger when public clinics run out of basic medicines (stockouts)?

options.A: Hospitals automatically receive double their budget allocation
options.B: Doctors start prescribing fewer medications to save money
options.C: Pharmaceutical companies lower their international prices
options.D: Patients lose trust and may buy unsafe drugs from roadside vendors

explanation: Exactly. When shelves are empty, desperate patients turn to the street, exposing themselves to dangerous counterfeit drugs.

question: What procurement practice helps health authorities buy essential medicines at a much lower cost?

options.A: Bulk purchasing using generic non-proprietary names
options.B: Ordering exclusively through expensive luxury suppliers
options.D: Buying small batches from local retail pharmacies daily

explanation: Great job! Buying large quantities of generics lets health systems take advantage of bulk discounts.

question: What does 'rational drug use' mean for a patient?

options.A: Every patient leaves the clinic with at least five different prescriptions
options.B: Patients receive the right drug, correct dose, and proper duration for their condition
options.C: Doctors prescribe the most expensive medication available on the market
options.D: Pharmacies clear out all their expiring stock within forty-eight hours

explanation: You got it! Rational use means matching the exact illness with a safe, cost-effective treatment without waste or misuse.

question: Why is the overuse and misuse of antibiotics a serious public health threat?

options.A: It accelerates the development of dangerous antimicrobial resistance
options.B: It permanently ruins hospital refrigeration and storage units
options.C: It causes patients to develop allergic reactions to all known foods
options.D: It immediately bankrupts national pharmaceutical manufacturing firms

explanation: Spot on! Misusing antibiotics teaches bacteria how to survive them, creating superbugs that are terribly hard to treat later.

question: A patient tells you they plan to stop their blood pressure medication as soon as they feel better. What should you as a nurse do?

options.A: Agree that stopping is fine since the symptoms have temporarily disappeared
options.B: Suggest they sell the remaining pills to a neighbor with similar symptoms
options.C: Explain that chronic conditions require ongoing treatment and counsel them on adherence
options.D: Tell them to double the dose tomorrow to finish the medication faster

explanation: Brilliant nursing judgment! Chronic illnesses need continuous management, and patient education is our superpower as nurses.

question: How can frontline nurses directly help prevent medicine wastage in health clinics?

options.A: By refusing to treat patients who cannot pay cash upfront
options.B: By maintaining accurate inventory records and monitoring expiration dates
options.C: By hiding extra drug supplies in private lockers for emergencies
options.D: By ordering random medications without checking clinic records

explanation: You got it! Keeping a close eye on stock and expiry dates ensures medicines are used properly before they spoil.
